claim: The great auk was once abundant and distributed across the North Atlantic.
source: The great auk was once abundant and distributed across the North Atlantic.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general characterization of the species' historical status.

claim: The great auk is now extinct.
source: It is now extinct, having been heavily exploited for its eggs, meat, and feathers.
evidence: This is a well-established fact stated in the abstract.

claim: The great auk was heavily exploited for its eggs, meat, and feathers.
source: It is now extinct, having been heavily exploited for its eggs, meat, and feathers.
evidence: This is stated as the reason for extinction in the abstract.

claim: Complete mitochondrial genomes of 41 individuals from across the species' geographic range were sequenced.
source: We sequenced complete mitochondrial genomes of 41 individuals from across the species' geographic range and reconstructed population structure and population dynamics throughout the Holocene.
evidence: This describes the primary data generated in the study.

claim: There is no evidence that great auks were at risk of extinction prior to the onset of intensive human hunting in the early 16th century.
source: Taken together, our data do not provide any evidence that great auks were at risk of extinction prior to the onset of intensive human hunting in the early 16th century.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the genetic analyses presented in the study.

claim: Human hunting alone could have been sufficient to cause the extinction of the great auk.
source: In addition, our population viability analyses reveal that even if the great auk had not been under threat by environmental change, human hunting alone could have been sufficient to cause its extinction.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the population viability analyses.

claim: The great auk (Pinguinus impennis) was a large, flightless diving bird thought to have once numbered in the millions.
source: The great auk (Pinguinus impennis) was a large, flightless diving bird thought to have once numbered in the millions (Birkhead, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Birkhead, 1993.

claim: The great auk is a member of the family Alcidae in the order Charadriiformes.
source: A member of the family Alcidae in the order Charadriiformes, its closest extant relative is the razorbill (Alca torda) (Moum et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a taxonomic classification supported by citation.

claim: The closest extant relative of the great auk is the razorbill (Alca torda).
source: A member of the family Alcidae in the order Charadriiformes, its closest extant relative is the razorbill (Alca torda) (Moum et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Moum et al., 2002.

claim: The great auk was distributed around the North Atlantic with breeding colonies along the east coast of North America, especially on the islands off Newfoundland.
source: The great auk was distributed around the North Atlantic and breeding colonies could be found along the east coast of North America, especially on the islands off Newfoundland (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1 showing geographic distribution.

claim: The great auk bred on islands off Iceland and Scotland.
source: The species also bred on islands off Iceland and Scotland, and was found throughout Scandinavia (Norway, Denmark, and Sweden), with evidence of bone finds existing as far south as Florida and in to the Mediterranean (Fuller, 1999; Grieve, 1885).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fuller, 1999 and Grieve, 1885.

claim: The great auk was found throughout Scandinavia (Norway, Denmark, and Sweden).
source: The species also bred on islands off Iceland and Scotland, and was found throughout Scandinavia (Norway, Denmark, and Sweden), with evidence of bone finds existing as far south as Florida and in to the Mediterranean (Fuller, 1999; Grieve, 1885).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fuller, 1999 and Grieve, 1885.

claim: Evidence of great auk bone finds exists as far south as Florida and into the Mediterranean.
source: The species also bred on islands off Iceland and Scotland, and was found throughout Scandinavia (Norway, Denmark, and Sweden), with evidence of bone finds existing as far south as Florida and in to the Mediterranean (Fuller, 1999; Grieve, 1885).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fuller, 1999 and Grieve, 1885.

claim: Great auks were hunted for their meat and eggs by the Beothuk in North America in prehistoric times.
source: In prehistoric times, they were hunted for their meat and eggs by the Beothuk in North America (Fuller, 1999; Gaskell, 2000), the Inuit of Greenland (Meldgaard, 1988), Scandinavians (Hufthammer, 1982), Icelanders (Bengtson, 1984), in Britain (Best, 2013; Best and Mulville, 2016), Magdalenian hunter-gatherers in the Bay of Biscay (Laroulandie et al., 2016), and possibly even Neanderthals (Halliday, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fuller, 1999 and Gaskell, 2000.

claim: Great auks were hunted by the Inuit of Greenland in prehistoric times.
source: In prehistoric times, they were hunted for their meat and eggs by the Beothuk in North America (Fuller, 1999; Gaskell, 2000), the Inuit of Greenland (Meldgaard, 1988), Scandinavians (Hufthammer, 1982), Icelanders (Bengtson, 1984), in Britain (Best, 2013; Best and Mulville, 2016), Magdalenian hunter-gatherers in the Bay of Biscay (Laroulandie et al., 2016), and possibly even Neanderthals (Halliday, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Meldgaard, 1988.

claim: Great auks were hunted by Scandinavians in prehistoric times.
source: In prehistoric times, they were hunted for their meat and eggs by the Beothuk in North America (Fuller, 1999; Gaskell, 2000), the Inuit of Greenland (Meldgaard, 1988), Scandinavians (Hufthammer, 1982), Icelanders (Bengtson, 1984), in Britain (Best, 2013; Best and Mulville, 2016), Magdalenian hunter-gatherers in the Bay of Biscay (Laroulandie et al., 2016), and possibly even Neanderthals (Halliday, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hufthammer, 1982.

claim: Great auks were hunted by Icelanders in prehistoric times.
source: In prehistoric times, they were hunted for their meat and eggs by the Beothuk in North America (Fuller, 1999; Gaskell, 2000), the Inuit of Greenland (Meldgaard, 1988), Scandinavians (Hufthammer, 1982), Icelanders (Bengtson, 1984), in Britain (Best, 2013; Best and Mulville, 2016), Magdalenian hunter-gatherers in the Bay of Biscay (Laroulandie et al., 2016), and possibly even Neanderthals (Halliday, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bengtson, 1984.

claim: Great auks were hunted in Britain in prehistoric times.
source: In prehistoric times, they were hunted for their meat and eggs by the Beothuk in North America (Fuller, 1999; Gaskell, 2000), the Inuit of Greenland (Meldgaard, 1988), Scandinavians (Hufthammer, 1982), Icelanders (Bengtson, 1984), in Britain (Best, 2013; Best and Mulville, 2016), Magdalenian hunter-gatherers in the Bay of Biscay (Laroulandie et al., 2016), and possibly even Neanderthals (Halliday, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Best, 2013 and Best and Mulville, 2016.

claim: Great auks were hunted by Magdalenian hunter-gatherers in the Bay of Biscay in prehistoric times.
source: In prehistoric times, they were hunted for their meat and eggs by the Beothuk in North America (Fuller, 1999; Gaskell, 2000), the Inuit of Greenland (Meldgaard, 1988), Scandinavians (Hufthammer, 1982), Icelanders (Bengtson, 1984), in Britain (Best, 2013; Best and Mulville, 2016), Magdalenian hunter-gatherers in the Bay of Biscay (Laroulandie et al., 2016), and possibly even Neanderthals (Halliday, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Laroulandie et al., 2016.

claim: Great auks were possibly hunted by Neanderthals.
source: In prehistoric times, they were hunted for their meat and eggs by the Beothuk in North America (Fuller, 1999; Gaskell, 2000), the Inuit of Greenland (Meldgaard, 1988), Scandinavians (Hufthammer, 1982), Icelanders (Bengtson, 1984), in Britain (Best, 2013; Best and Mulville, 2016), Magdalenian hunter-gatherers in the Bay of Biscay (Laroulandie et al., 2016), and possibly even Neanderthals (Halliday, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Halliday, 1978, but noted as speculative ('possibly').

claim: Around 1500 AD intensive hunting of great auks began by European seamen visiting the fishing grounds of Newfoundland.
source: Around 1500 AD intensive hunting began by European seamen visiting the fishing grounds of Newfoundland (Bengtson, 1984; Fuller, 1999; Gaskell, 2000; Steenstrup, 1855).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Towards the end of the 1700s, the development of commercial hunting for the feather trade intensified exploitation levels of great auks.
source: Towards the end of the 1700s, the development of commercial hunting for the feather trade intensified exploitation levels (Fuller, 1999; Gaskell, 2000; Kirkham and Montevecchi, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: As their rarity increased, great auk specimens and eggs became desirable for private and institutional collections.
source: As their rarity increased, great auk specimens and eggs became desirable for private and institutional collections.
evidence: This is stated as a historical fact in the introduction.

claim: The last reliably recorded breeding pair of great auks were killed in June 1844 on Eldey Island, Iceland, to be added to a museum collection.
source: The last reliably recorded breeding pair were killed in June 1844 on Eldey Island, Iceland, to be added to a museum collection (Bengtson, 1984; Fuller, 1999; Gaskell, 2000; Grieve, 1885; Newton, 1861; Steenstrup, 1855; Thomas et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: There are scattered records of great auks dating to later than 1844, including in 1848 near Vardø, Norway.
source: There are scattered records of great auks dating to later than 1844, including in 1848 near Vardø, Norway (Fuller, 1999; Newton, 1861), and 1852 in Newfoundland (Fuller, 1999; Grieve, 1885; Newton, 1861).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: There are scattered records of great auks in 1852 in Newfoundland.
source: There are scattered records of great auks dating to later than 1844, including in 1848 near Vardø, Norway (Fuller, 1999; Newton, 1861), and 1852 in Newfoundland (Fuller, 1999; Grieve, 1885; Newton, 1861).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: BirdLife International/IUCN recognises the last sighting of great auk as 1852.
source: BirdLife International/IUCN recognises the last sighting as 1852 (BirdLife International, 2016a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to BirdLife International, 2016a.

claim: Uncertainty remains about the reliability of all great auk sightings after 1844.
source: However, uncertainty remains about the reliability of all of these later sightings (Fuller, 1999; Grieve, 1885).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: There is little doubt that the extensive hunting pressure on the species contributed significantly to its demise.
source: There is little doubt that the extensive hunting pressure on the species contributed significantly to its demise.
evidence: This is stated as a consensus view in the introduction.

claim: It is unclear whether hunting alone could have been responsible for the demise of the great auk, or whether the species was already in decline due to non-anthropogenic environmental changes.
source: Nevertheless, despite the well documented history of exploitation since the 16th century, it is unclear whether hunting alone could have been responsible for the demise of the great auk, or whether the species was already in decline due to non-anthropogenic environmental changes (Bengtson, 1984; Birkhead, 1993; Fuller, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents the research question of the study.

claim: There is evidence of a decrease in great auk numbers on the eastern side of the North Atlantic, as reflected in a decline in bone finds in England, Scotland, and Scandinavia.
source: For example, there is evidence of a decrease in great auk numbers on the eastern side of the North Atlantic, as reflected in a decline in bone finds in England, Scotland, and Scandinavia, which remains unexplained and could have been caused by hunting as well as environmental change (Bengtson, 1984; Best and Mulville, 2014; Grieve, 1885; Hufthammer, 1982; Serjeantson, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: If the great auk had been at risk of extinction prior to the onset of intensive hunting in the 16th century, we would expect to see genetic signatures of population decline, including limited genetic diversity and pronounced population structure.
source: However, if the species had been at risk of extinction prior to the onset of intensive hunting in the 16th century, we would expect to see genetic signatures of population decline, including limited genetic diversity and pronounced population structure.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on established genetic principles.

claim: The lack of an observable loss in genetic diversity during the last few centuries prior to the extinction would be consistent with a rapid demographic decline at the end.
source: In contrast, the lack of an observable loss in genetic diversity during the last few centuries prior to the extinction would be consistent with a rapid demographic decline at the end.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on established genetic principles.

claim: Human hunting alone can only be considered a reasonable explanation for the extinction of the great auk if population viability analyses show that extinction could have been caused by harvest rates that would have been realistic for the time and circumstances of the harvest.
source: At the same time, human hunting alone can only be considered a reasonable explanation for the extinction of the great auk, if population viability analyses show that extinction could have been caused by harvest rates that would have been realistic for the time and circumstances of the harvest.
evidence: This is a logical statement about the requirements for supporting the hunting-only hypothesis.

claim: Using hybridisation capture combined with high-throughput sequencing, sequence data were generated from 66 bone samples of great auk.
source: Using hybridisation capture combined with high-throughput sequencing, we generated short-read sequence data from 66 bone samples of great auk (See Supplementary file 1a for sample information).
evidence: This describes the methods and data generated in the study.

claim: Following read processing and filtering, 35 samples passed the quality requirements and were suitable for further analysis.
source: Following read processing and filtering, 35 samples passed the quality requirements (see Materials and methods) and were suitable for further analysis.
evidence: This describes the data processing results.

claim: Six previously published mitogenome sequences from tissue or feather samples were included in the analysis.
source: In addition to the sequences generated from bones, we included six previously published mitogenome sequences from tissue or feather samples (Thomas et al., 2017) (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This describes data sources used in the study.

claim: The combined data set comprised 41 complete mitogenomes, representing individuals from across the former range of the great auk and spanning the period 170–15,000 years before present.
source: The combined data set comprised 41 complete mitogenomes, representing individuals from across the former range of the great auk and spanning the period 170–15,000 years before present (ybp).
evidence: This describes the final dataset used in the study.

claim: For samples in the final data set, the mean average read length of aligned bases to the reference great auk mitogenome was 55.12 base pairs, with a range of 41.21–86.95 bp.
source: For samples in the final data set, the mean average read length of aligned bases to the reference great auk mitogenome (GenBank accession KU158188.1 [Anmarkrud and Lifjeld, 2017]) was 55.12 base pairs (bp), with a range of 41.21–86.95 bp.
evidence: This describes the sequencing data characteristics.

claim: Unique mitogenome coverage of samples ranged from 6.39 × to 430.09×, with average coverage of 72.5×.
source: Unique mitogenome coverage of these samples ranged from 6.39 × to 430.09×, with average coverage of 72.5× (Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This describes the sequencing coverage achieved.

claim: The final alignment length was 16,641 bp, including 9994 bp (after removal of gaps) that were shared across all 41 mitogenomes.
source: The final alignment length was 16,641 bp, including 9994 bp (after removal of gaps) that were shared across all 41 mitogenomes.
evidence: This describes the alignment characteristics.

claim: Haplotype diversity among the great auk mitogenomes was high, with only two individuals yielding identical haplotypes across the 9994 bp covered by all 41 mitogenomes.
source: Haplotype diversity among the great auk mitogenomes was high, with only two individuals yielding identical haplotypes across the 9994 bp covered by all 41 mitogenomes.
evidence: This is a result from the genetic diversity analysis.

claim: The two identical sequences differed in age, so that when divided into different age groups, each age group contained a unique set of haplotypes.
source: The two identical sequences differed in age, so that when divided into different age groups, each age group contained a unique set of haplotypes.
evidence: This is a result from the genetic diversity analysis.

claim: No reduction of haplotype diversity could be identified in more recent samples.
source: No reduction of haplotype diversity could be identified in more recent samples (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a result from the genetic diversity analysis, supported by Figure 2.

claim: No structure in the distribution of haplotypes was observed using Bayesian analyses using BEAST, maximum-likelihood phylogenetic analysis using RAxML, statistical parsimony network analysis using TempNet, or median-joining network analysis using PopART.
source: We observed no structure in the distribution of haplotypes using any of our four approaches to reconstruct phylogeographic and temporal relationships among the samples: Bayesian analyses using BEAST (Appendix 1—figure 1 and Appendix 1—figure 2); maximum-likelihood phylogenetic analysis using RAxML; statistical parsimony network analysis using TempNet (Figure 2); and median-joining network analysis using PopART (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a result from multiple phylogenetic and network analyses.

claim: GPS-equipped drifting capsules were deployed in the North Atlantic as part of the 'Message in a Bottle' project by Verkís Consulting Engineers.
source: To evaluate potential reasons for the observed lack of population structure, we sourced data from GPS-equipped drifting capsules that had been deployed in the North Atlantic as part of the 'Message in a Bottle' project by Verkís Consulting Engineers.
evidence: This describes the source of ocean current data used in the study.

claim: The route taken by the GPS capsules connects some of the main breeding colonies in St Kilda (Scotland), Geirfuglasker/Eldey Island (Iceland), and Funk Island (Canada).
source: The route taken by the capsules connects some of the main breeding colonies in St Kilda (Scotland), Geirfuglasker/Eldey Island (Iceland), and Funk Island (Canada) (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a result from the GPS capsule tracking data, shown in Figure 4.

claim: The demographic history of the great auk was reconstructed using the 25 dated mitogenomes and found support for a constant population size through time, with no evidence of a population decline.
source: We reconstructed the demographic history of the great auk using the 25 dated mitogenomes (see Materials and Methods for definition of 'dated' samples) and found support for a constant population size through time, with no evidence of a population decline.
evidence: This is a primary result from the demographic analysis.

claim: The most recent common ancestor of the great auk samples was dated to 42,188 ybp (95% credibility interval 24,743–84,894 ybp).
source: Despite having a high haplotype diversity, our samples had a shallow divergence and their most recent common ancestor was dated to 42,188 ybp (95% credibility interval 24,743–84,894 ybp; see Appendix 3).
evidence: This is a result from the Bayesian phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The effective female population size (Nef) was estimated at 9558 (95% credibility interval 4548–19,665), assuming a generation interval of 12 years.
source: The effective female population size (Nef) was estimated at 9558 (95% credibility interval 4548–19,665), assuming a generation interval of 12 years (BirdLife International, 2016a).
evidence: This is a result from the demographic analysis.

claim: A second analysis including the undated samples also yielded support for a constant population size, with an effective female population size of 7331 (95% credibility interval 2477–19,492).
source: To examine the effect of including the undated samples, we repeated the analysis on the complete data set while accounting for the uncertainty in the ages of the undated samples. This second analysis also yielded support for a constant population size, with an effective female population size of 7331 (95% credibility interval 2477–19,492).
evidence: This is a result from the demographic analysis with extended dataset.

claim: Census size (Nc) estimates based on the effective population size and the range of known Ne/Nc ratios yielded an expectedly wide range of 12,292–756,346 individuals.
source: Census size (Nc) estimates based on the effective population size and the range of known Ne/Nc ratios (Frankham, 1995) yielded an expectedly wide range of 12,292–756,346 individuals.
evidence: This is a result from converting effective population size to census size using published ratios.

claim: Under conservative settings, annual harvest rates up to 9% of the pre-hunting population were sustainable.
source: We found that under our conservative settings, annual harvest rates up to 9% of the pre-hunting population were sustainable.
evidence: This is a result from the population viability analysis.

claim: For a pre-hunting population size of 2 million individuals, a 9% annual harvest rate corresponds to an annual harvest rate of 180,000 birds.
source: For example, for a pre-hunting population size of 2 million individuals, this corresponds to an annual harvest rate of 180,000 birds.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the population viability analysis results.

claim: An annual harvest rate of 10% of the pre-hunting population combined with an annual egg harvest rate of 5% led to extinction in a large proportion of simulations.
source: In contrast, an annual harvest rate of 10% of the pre-hunting population combined with an annual egg harvest rate of 5% led to extinction in a large proportion of our simulations.
evidence: This is a result from the population viability analysis.

claim: A harvest rate of 10.5% (egg harvest rate 5%) of the pre-hunting population led to extinction within 350 years in all simulations.
source: A harvest rate of 10.5% (egg harvest rate 5%) of the pre-hunting population led to extinction within 350 years in all of our simulations.
evidence: This is a result from the population viability analysis.

claim: Assuming a density-dependent reduction of mortality had only a small effect on sustainable harvest rates.
source: Assuming a density-dependent reduction of mortality had only a small effect on sustainable harvest rates (Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from the population viability analysis, shown in Table 1.

claim: Even if no eggs at all were harvested, the population was still at risk of extinction at 10.5% bird harvest rate, with extinction probabilities between 15% and 81%.
source: Furthermore, even if no eggs at all were harvested, the population was still at risk of extinction at 10.5% bird harvest rate, with extinction probabilities between 15% (population size 6 million, density-dependent mortality) and 81% (population size 6 million, no density-dependent mortality, [Table 1]).
evidence: This is a result from the population viability analysis, shown in Table 1.

claim: When using the much higher mortality rate of the razorbill, with a starting population of 2 million birds and slightly more realistic settings for reproductive age and success, harvest rates are only sustainable up to about 40,000 birds per year even if no eggs are harvested and mortality is gradually reduced to 50% of the starting value as the population density declines.
source: For comparison, when using the much higher mortality rate of the razorbill, with a starting population of 2 million birds and slightly more realistic settings for reproductive age and success, harvest rates are only sustainable up to about 40,000 birds per year even if no eggs are harvested and mortality is gradually reduced to 50% of the starting value as the population density declines (see Supplementary file 2b).
evidence: This is a result from the population viability analysis using razorbill parameters.

claim: The analyses of the demographic history of great auks support a constant population size within the temporal resolution of the data (back to the most recent common ancestor of all samples 24,000–85,000 ybp).
source: Our analyses of the demographic history of great auks support a constant population size within the temporal resolution of our data (back to the most recent common ancestor of all samples 24,000–85,000 ybp).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the demographic analysis.

claim: No evidence of a decline in the great auk population prior to the onset of intensive hunting was found.
source: Therefore, we find no evidence of a decline in the population prior to the onset of intensive hunting.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the demographic analysis.

claim: High haplotype diversity was observed across the sampling period, right up to the demise of the species.
source: We also observed high haplotype diversity across the sampling period, right up to the demise of the species.
evidence: This is a result from the genetic diversity analysis.

claim: If the great auk had been at risk of extinction prior to the onset of intensive human hunting, we would expect to see genetic evidence of such stress, as observed in studies of cave bears and bison.
source: If the great auk had been at risk of extinction prior to the onset of intensive human hunting, for example as a result of long-term suboptimal habitat or environmental change, we would expect to see genetic evidence of such stress, as for example observed in studies of cave bears (Stiller et al., 2010) and bison (Shapiro et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on comparisons with other species, supported by citations.

claim: If the population declined rapidly, genetic data would have only very limited power to detect such a decline in a long-lived species.
source: If, on the other hand, the population declined rapidly, for example as a result of extensive hunting, genetic data would have only very limited power to detect such a decline in a long-lived species.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of genetic data for detecting rapid declines.

claim: Mitochondrial DNA studies of New Zealand moa found no evidence of a population decline prior to extinction.
source: Mitochondrial DNA studies of New Zealand moa found no evidence of a population decline prior to extinction (Allentoft et al., 2014; Rawlence et al., 2012) and a study of the endemic Hawaiian Petrel came to a similar conclusion (Welch et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to other studies.

claim: A study of the endemic Hawaiian Petrel found no evidence of a population decline prior to extinction.
source: Mitochondrial DNA studies of New Zealand moa found no evidence of a population decline prior to extinction (Allentoft et al., 2014; Rawlence et al., 2012) and a study of the endemic Hawaiian Petrel came to a similar conclusion (Welch et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Welch et al., 2012.

claim: A recent whole-genome study of two extinct New Zealand songbirds (huia and South Island kõkako), which disappeared after human settlement within 700 years, found no genetic evidence of population decline prior to the disappearance of the species.
source: In fact, even a recent whole-genome study of two extinct New Zealand songbirds (huia and South Island kõkako), which disappeared after human settlement within 700 years, found no genetic evidence of population decline prior to the disappearance of the species (Dussex et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dussex et al., 2019.

claim: The results are consistent with a rapid decline of great auks.
source: Therefore, our results are consistent with a rapid decline of great auks.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic analyses.

claim: The results indicate that the demise of the great auk was beyond the detection limit of genetic data.
source: It is important to keep in mind, though, that our results simply indicate that the demise of the great auk was beyond the detection limit of genetic data.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the genetic analysis.

claim: The results do not necessarily confirm whether the rapid demise that must have taken place prior to extinction started before or after the onset of extensive human hunting.
source: They do not necessarily confirm whether the rapid demise that must have taken place prior to extinction started before or after the onset of extensive human hunting, nor do the results provide an indication of whether there was more than one population decline.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the conclusions.

claim: A localised, unexplained decline in great auk numbers on the eastern side of the North Atlantic over the past 2,000 years, inferred from a decline in bone finds in England, Scotland, and Scandinavia, does not appear to have been severe enough to leave a genetic signature.
source: A localised, unexplained decline in great auk numbers on the eastern side of the North Atlantic over the past 2,000 years, for example, which has been inferred from a decline in bone finds in England, Scotland, and Scandinavia (Bengtson, 1984; Best and Mulville, 2014; Grieve, 1885; Hufthammer, 1982; Serjeantson, 2001), does not appear to have been severe enough to leave a genetic signature.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic analyses in the context of archaeological evidence.

claim: The discrepancy between effective and census population size suggests that the species went through a severe bottleneck in the recent past.
source: This is noteworthy because it suggests that the species went through a severe bottleneck in the recent past.
evidence: This is an inference from the population size estimates.

claim: The shallow divergence of less than 90,000 years between the sequenced individuals suggests a population decline in the late Pleistocene, potentially associated with climate fluctuations.
source: The shallow divergence of less than 90,000 years between the sequenced individuals suggests a population decline in the late Pleistocene, potentially associated with climate fluctuations.
evidence: This is an inference from the divergence time estimates.

claim: The wide 95% credibility intervals of divergence-time estimates prevent narrowing down the cause of the bottleneck to any specific event.
source: However, the wide 95% credibility intervals of our divergence-time estimates prevent us from narrowing down the cause of the bottleneck to any specific event.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the analysis.

claim: The high percentage of singleton haplotypes in the data is characteristic of a population expansion following a bottleneck.
source: In any case, the high percentage of singleton haplotypes in our data, which is characteristic of a population expansion following a bottleneck (Slatkin and Hudson, 1991), together with the large census size at the onset of intensive hunting, suggest that the great auk had successfully recovered from the bottleneck.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the genetic data supported by citation.

claim: The large census size at the onset of intensive hunting suggests that the great auk had successfully recovered from the bottleneck.
source: In any case, the high percentage of singleton haplotypes in our data, which is characteristic of a population expansion following a bottleneck (Slatkin and Hudson, 1991), together with the large census size at the onset of intensive hunting, suggest that the great auk had successfully recovered from the bottleneck.
evidence: This is an inference from the genetic data and historical records.

claim: Genetic analyses failed to detect any female population structure in space or time.
source: Our genetic analyses failed to detect any female population structure in space or time, indicating a lack of marked barriers to dispersal among populations across the species' range.
evidence: This is a result from the population structure analyses.

claim: The lack of population structure indicates a lack of marked barriers to dispersal among populations across the species' range.
source: Our genetic analyses failed to detect any female population structure in space or time, indicating a lack of marked barriers to dispersal among populations across the species' range.
evidence: This is an inference from the lack of population structure.

claim: The lack of population structure is inconsistent with predictions of limited or no interbreeding between populations from either side of the North Atlantic.
source: This is inconsistent with predictions of limited or no interbreeding between populations from either side of the North Atlantic (Burness and Montevecchi, 1992), and suspected regional philopatry in this species (Bengtson, 1984; Montevecchi and Kirk, 1996).
evidence: This is a comparison of the results with previous predictions, supported by citations.

claim: The lack of population structure is inconsistent with suspected regional philopatry in the great auk.
source: This is inconsistent with predictions of limited or no interbreeding between populations from either side of the North Atlantic (Burness and Montevecchi, 1992), and suspected regional philopatry in this species (Bengtson, 1984; Montevecchi and Kirk, 1996).
evidence: This is a comparison of the results with previous predictions, supported by citations.

claim: Lack of population structure is common in seabirds.
source: Such a lack of structure is, however, common in seabirds, and has been observed in several relatives of the great auk, such as the thick-billed murre (Uria lomvia; no structure within ocean basins) (Tigano et al., 2015), common murre (Uria aalge; structure in the Atlantic but not in the Pacific) (Morris-Pocock et al., 2008), ancient murrelets (Synthliboramphus antiquus; no genetic differentiation in the North Pacific) (Pearce et al., 2009), and little auk (Alle alle; no structure in the Arctic) (Wojczulanis-Jakubas et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies of related species.

claim: The thick-billed murre (Uria lomvia) shows no structure within ocean basins.
source: Such a lack of structure is, however, common in seabirds, and has been observed in several relatives of the great auk, such as the thick-billed murre (Uria lomvia; no structure within ocean basins) (Tigano et al., 2015), common murre (Uria aalge; structure in the Atlantic but not in the Pacific) (Morris-Pocock et al., 2008), ancient murrelets (Synthliboramphus antiquus; no genetic differentiation in the North Pacific) (Pearce et al., 2009), and little auk (Alle alle; no structure in the Arctic) (Wojczulanis-Jakubas et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tigano et al., 2015.

claim: The common murre (Uria aalge) shows structure in the Atlantic but not in the Pacific.
source: Such a lack of structure is, however, common in seabirds, and has been observed in several relatives of the great auk, such as the thick-billed murre (Uria lomvia; no structure within ocean basins) (Tigano et al., 2015), common murre (Uria aalge; structure in the Atlantic but not in the Pacific) (Morris-Pocock et al., 2008), ancient murrelets (Synthliboramphus antiquus; no genetic differentiation in the North Pacific) (Pearce et al., 2009), and little auk (Alle alle; no structure in the Arctic) (Wojczulanis-Jakubas et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Morris-Pocock et al., 2008.

claim: Ancient murrelets (Synthliboramphus antiquus) show no genetic differentiation in the North Pacific.
source: Such a lack of structure is, however, common in seabirds, and has been observed in several relatives of the great auk, such as the thick-billed murre (Uria lomvia; no structure within ocean basins) (Tigano et al., 2015), common murre (Uria aalge; structure in the Atlantic but not in the Pacific) (Morris-Pocock et al., 2008), ancient murrelets (Synthliboramphus antiquus; no genetic differentiation in the North Pacific) (Pearce et al., 2009), and little auk (Alle alle; no structure in the Arctic) (Wojczulanis-Jakubas et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pearce et al., 2009.

claim: The little auk (Alle alle) shows no structure in the Arctic.
source: Such a lack of structure is, however, common in seabirds, and has been observed in several relatives of the great auk, such as the thick-billed murre (Uria lomvia; no structure within ocean basins) (Tigano et al., 2015), common murre (Uria aalge; structure in the Atlantic but not in the Pacific) (Morris-Pocock et al., 2008), ancient murrelets (Synthliboramphus antiquus; no genetic differentiation in the North Pacific) (Pearce et al., 2009), and little auk (Alle alle; no structure in the Arctic) (Wojczulanis-Jakubas et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wojczulanis-Jakubas et al., 2014.

claim: Little or no population structure has been reported for the emperor penguin (Aptenodytes forsteri).
source: For example, little or no population structure has been reported for the emperor penguin (Aptenodytes forsteri) (Cristofari et al., 2016), chinstrap penguin (Pygoscelis antarcticus) (Mura-Jornet et al., 2018), and Adélie penguin (P. adeliae) (Gorman et al., 2017; Roeder et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cristofari et al., 2016.

claim: Little or no population structure has been reported for the chinstrap penguin (Pygoscelis antarcticus).
source: For example, little or no population structure has been reported for the emperor penguin (Aptenodytes forsteri) (Cristofari et al., 2016), chinstrap penguin (Pygoscelis antarcticus) (Mura-Jornet et al., 2018), and Adélie penguin (P. adeliae) (Gorman et al., 2017; Roeder et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mura-Jornet et al., 2018.

claim: Little or no population structure has been reported for the Adélie penguin (P. adeliae).
source: For example, little or no population structure has been reported for the emperor penguin (Aptenodytes forsteri) (Cristofari et al., 2016), chinstrap penguin (Pygoscelis antarcticus) (Mura-Jornet et al., 2018), and Adélie penguin (P. adeliae) (Gorman et al., 2017; Roeder et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gorman et al., 2017 and Roeder et al., 2001.

claim: It has been suggested that migrations occurred in both northward and southward directions between breeding and wintering sites, aided by ocean currents such as the East Greenland Current.
source: It has been suggested that migrations occurred in both northward and southward directions between breeding and wintering sites, aided by ocean currents such as the East Greenland Current (Brown, 1985; Meldgaard, 1988; Montevecchi and Kirk, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: High vagility of the great auk is supported by its ability to track its habitat in response to climate change, as evidenced by archaeological records.
source: Nevertheless, high vagility of the great auk is further supported by its ability to track its habitat in response to climate change, as evidenced by archaeological records (Bengtson, 1984; Campmas et al., 2010; Meldgaard, 1988; Serjeantson, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to archaeological studies.

claim: No evidence was found in the genetic data that would suggest that great auk populations were at risk of extinction at the time when human hunting intensified.
source: We find no evidence in our genetic data that would suggest that great auk populations were at risk of extinction at the time when human hunting intensified.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the genetic analyses.

claim: The mitochondrial genome is only a single genetic marker and the samples were insufficiently preserved to yield nuclear SNP data.
source: The mitochondrial genome is only a single genetic marker and our samples were insufficiently preserved to yield nuclear SNP data (Appendix 9), which would have offered a greater degree of resolution with the potential to detect population structure.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the study.

claim: As a result of limitations in sample preservation and availability, the sample size of 41 is relatively small for population genetic analysis and could have limited the ability to resolve changes in population structure and size.
source: Similarly, as a result of limitations in sample preservation and availability, the sample size of 41 is relatively small for population genetic analysis and could have limited our ability to resolve changes in population structure and size.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the study.

claim: Population viability analysis shows that harvest rates that would cause extinction under all of the conditions explored in the simulations are well below reasonable estimates of harvest rates as inferred from historical sources.
source: Our population viability analysis shows that, independent of the population size, harvest rates that would cause extinction under all of the conditions explored in our simulations are well below reasonable estimates of harvest rates as inferred from historical sources.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the population viability analysis.

claim: A total population size of 2 million birds corresponds to 1 million mature individuals.
source: For example, a total population size of 2 million birds corresponds to 1 million mature individuals.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the population viability analysis parameters.

claim: At a census size of 2 million birds, an annual harvest of 210,000 birds and fewer than 26,000 eggs would have caused the extinction of the great auk within 350 years.
source: At this census size, an annual harvest of 210,000 birds and fewer than 26,000 eggs would have caused the extinction of the great auk within 350 years.
evidence: This is a result from the population viability analysis.

claim: Actual hunting pressure on great auks is likely to have far exceeded 210,000 birds annually.
source: Actual hunting pressure on great auks is likely to have far exceeded 210,000 birds annually.
evidence: This is an inference based on historical records discussed in the following text.

claim: From 1497 AD, when Europeans discovered the rich fishing grounds of Newfoundland, fleets of 300 to 400 ships from various European countries were drawn annually to this region.
source: From 1497 AD, when Europeans discovered the rich fishing grounds of Newfoundland, fleets of 300 to 400 ships from various European countries were drawn annually to this region, which is likely to have had the highest population density of great auks (Bengtson, 1984; Steenstrup, 1855).
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical sources.

claim: The Newfoundland region is likely to have had the highest population density of great auks.
source: From 1497 AD, when Europeans discovered the rich fishing grounds of Newfoundland, fleets of 300 to 400 ships from various European countries were drawn annually to this region, which is likely to have had the highest population density of great auks (Bengtson, 1984; Steenstrup, 1855).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Fishing stations were set up near colonies of the great auk and other seabirds, and these colonies were heavily exploited.
source: Fishing stations were set up near colonies of the great auk and other seabirds, and these colonies were heavily exploited (Pope, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pope, 2009.

claim: Great auks were likely to have been caught by fishing lines and in fishing nets.
source: Great auks were also likely to have been caught by fishing lines and in fishing nets (Montevecchi and Kirk, 1996; Piatt and Nettleship, 1985; Piatt and Nettleship, 1987; Pope, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Contemporary reports document a case in which approximately 1000 great auks were caught and killed within half an hour by two fishing vessels off the coast of Funk Island.
source: Contemporary reports document a case in which approximately 1000 great auks were caught and killed within half an hour by two fishing vessels off the coast of Funk Island (Bengtson, 1984; Grieve, 1885).
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical sources.

claim: If each of the 400 vessels in the Newfoundland region spent only half an hour a year harvesting great auks at the rate of 1000 birds per half hour, that would correspond to 200,000 birds a year.
source: Thus, if each of the 400 vessels in the region spent only half an hour a year harvesting great auks at this rate, that would already correspond to 200,000 birds a year.
evidence: This is a calculation based on historical records.

claim: At a total population size of 6 million birds, an annual harvest of 630,000 birds and 77,000 eggs would cause certain extinction.
source: At a total population size of 6 million birds, corresponding to the estimated 3 million mature individuals of common murre and thick-billed murre in the North Atlantic, an annual harvest of 630,000 birds and 77,000 eggs would cause certain extinction.
evidence: This is a result from the population viability analysis.

claim: Great auks were targeted for the feather trade, with hunters living on Funk Island throughout the summer with the purpose of killing the birds.
source: Even this number does not appear unrealistically high when considering that great auks were also targeted for the feather trade, with hunters living on Funk Island throughout the summer with the purpose of killing the birds (Gaskell, 2000; Kirkham and Montevecchi, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The great auk laid only one egg a year, which was not replaced if removed.
source: Adding to the effects of excessive hunting, the great auk laid only one egg a year, which was not replaced if removed (Bengtson, 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bengtson, 1984.

claim: Replenishing the large number of birds lost annually would have been highly improbable.
source: Thus, replenishing the large number of birds lost annually would have been highly improbable (Gaskell, 2000).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation.

claim: The estimates of harvest rates leading to extinction are likely to be conservatively high, because they are based on some unrealistically optimistic assumptions.
source: Critically, our estimates of harvest rates leading to extinction are likely to be conservatively high, because they are based on some unrealistically optimistic assumptions.
evidence: This is a statement about the conservative nature of the simulations.

claim: The simulation settings assume that 100% of mature birds breed, that they had 100% breeding success, and that their offspring was independent from the time the egg was laid.
source: For example, our settings assume that 100% of mature birds breed, that they had 100% breeding success, and that their offspring was independent from the time the egg was laid (hence no negative effect of parents being killed).
evidence: This describes the assumptions used in the population viability analysis.

claim: The simulations assumed the lowest natural mortality observed among all alcids for each age class.
source: Furthermore, we assumed the lowest natural mortality observed among all alcids for each age class and in some simulations reduced these mortality rates by half when population density declined, thereby considering the positive effects of increased availability of resources and reduced competition.
evidence: This describes the assumptions used in the population viability analysis.

claim: In some simulations, mortality rates were reduced by half when population density declined, thereby considering the positive effects of increased availability of resources and reduced competition.
source: Furthermore, we assumed the lowest natural mortality observed among all alcids for each age class and in some simulations reduced these mortality rates by half when population density declined, thereby considering the positive effects of increased availability of resources and reduced competition.
evidence: This describes the assumptions used in the population viability analysis.

claim: Detrimental effects of small population sizes, such as inbreeding depression, were not included in the simulations.
source: Detrimental effects of small population sizes, such as inbreeding depression, were not included in our simulations.
evidence: This describes the limitations of the population viability analysis.

claim: Using conservative settings brings an increased risk of overestimating the number of birds that could have been sustainably harvested.
source: However, this brings an increased risk of overestimating the number of birds that could have been sustainably harvested.
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of the conservative assumptions.

claim: Using the mortality rate of the razorbill and allowing for more variation in reproductive success reduces the sustainable harvest rate for a population of 2 million birds to as few as 40,000 birds per year.
source: Using the mortality rate of the razorbill and allowing for more variation in reproductive success (see Supplementary file 2a) reduces the sustainable harvest rate for a population of 2 million birds to as few as 40,000 birds per year.
evidence: This is a result from the population viability analysis using razorbill parameters.

claim: The razorbill can produce a second egg per season if the first one is lost.
source: However, the razorbill can produce a second egg per season if the first one is lost, so applying razorbill mortality rates to the great auk likely leads to an underestimation of the sustainable harvest rate.
evidence: This is a statement about razorbill biology.

claim: Applying razorbill mortality rates to the great auk likely leads to an underestimation of the sustainable harvest rate.
source: However, the razorbill can produce a second egg per season if the first one is lost, so applying razorbill mortality rates to the great auk likely leads to an underestimation of the sustainable harvest rate.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of using razorbill parameters.

claim: The conservative simulations require high harvest rates to cause the extinction of the great auk, but these values are largely consistent with harvest rates for present-day species.
source: Our conservative simulations require high harvest rates to cause the extinction of the great auk, but these values are largely consistent with harvest rates for present-day species.
evidence: This is a comparison of the simulation results with modern harvest rates.

claim: Until recently, between 200,000 and 300,000 murres (Uria spp.) were killed legally every year off the eastern Canadian coast.
source: For example, until recently, between 200,000 and 300,000 murres (Uria spp.) were killed legally every year off the eastern Canadian coast (Wilhelm et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wilhelm et al., 2008.

claim: Harvest rates were even higher before the mid-1990s, when between 300,000 and 700,000 thick-billed murres alone were being harvested annually.
source: Harvest rates were even higher before the mid-1990s, when between 300,000 and 700,000 thick-billed murres alone were being harvested annually (Wilhelm et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wilhelm et al., 2008.

claim: In Iceland, 150,000 to 233,000 Atlantic puffins were once killed annually, representing about 2–3% of the population.
source: In Iceland, 150,000 to 233,000 Atlantic puffins were once killed annually, representing about 2–3% of the population.
evidence: This is stated as a historical fact.

claim: 25–30% of the populations of species of black-backed gulls are killed annually.
source: In contrast, 25–30% of the populations of species of black-backed gulls are killed annually (Merkel and Barry, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Merkel and Barry, 2008.

claim: Current figures for annual harvest rates of auk species are considerably lower than historical rates and continue to decline.
source: Although current figures for annual harvest rates of auk species are considerably lower than those given above and continue to decline (e.g.,~25,000 puffins were killed in Iceland in 2016 compared with ~233,000 in 1995 [Statistics Iceland, 2016]; also see Frederiksen et al., 2016), the harvesting rates required to cause the extinction of the great auk would not be considered excessive even by modern standards.
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: About 25,000 puffins were killed in Iceland in 2016 compared with about 233,000 in 1995.
source: Although current figures for annual harvest rates of auk species are considerably lower than those given above and continue to decline (e.g.,~25,000 puffins were killed in Iceland in 2016 compared with ~233,000 in 1995 [Statistics Iceland, 2016]; also see Frederiksen et al., 2016), the harvesting rates required to cause the extinction of the great auk would not be considered excessive even by modern standards.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Statistics Iceland, 2016.

claim: The harvesting rates required to cause the extinction of the great auk would not be considered excessive even by modern standards.
source: Although current figures for annual harvest rates of auk species are considerably lower than those given above and continue to decline (e.g.,~25,000 puffins were killed in Iceland in 2016 compared with ~233,000 in 1995 [Statistics Iceland, 2016]; also see Frederiksen et al., 2016), the harvesting rates required to cause the extinction of the great auk would not be considered excessive even by modern standards.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the simulation results with modern harvest rates.

claim: Little evidence was found that the great auk was at risk of extinction prior to the onset of intensive human hunting.
source: In contrast with most studies of Pleistocene extinctions, which have argued for at least some level of climate-driven environmental contributions to species extinction, we have found little evidence that the great auk was at risk of extinction prior to the onset of intensive human hunting.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: The study does not provide unequivocal evidence that humans alone were the cause of great auk extinction.
source: Critically, this does not mean that our study provides unequivocal evidence that humans alone were the cause of great auk extinction.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the conclusions.

claim: To test the hypothesis that humans alone caused great auk extinction, simulations of great auk population dynamics in response to environmental change throughout the Holocene would be required.
source: To test this hypothesis, simulations of great auk population dynamics in response to environmental change throughout the Holocene would be required.
evidence: This is a statement about what would be needed to definitively test the hypothesis.

claim: With little information about great auk biology, simulations of population dynamics in response to environmental change would be highly speculative.
source: However, with little information about great auk biology, such simulations would be highly speculative.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of what can be concluded.

claim: The study has demonstrated that human hunting pressure alone was very likely to have been high enough to cause extinction even if the great auk population was not already under threat of extinction through environmental change.
source: What our study has demonstrated though, is that human hunting pressure alone was very likely to have been high enough to cause extinction even if the great auk population was not already under threat of extinction through environmental change.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: Industrial-scale commercial exploitation of natural resources has the potential to drive even an abundant, wide-ranging, highly vagile, and genetically diverse species to extinction within a short period of time.
source: Our findings highlight how industrial-scale commercial exploitation of natural resources have the potential to drive even an abundant, wide-ranging, highly vagile, and genetically diverse species to extinction within a short period of time.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the study.

claim: The findings echo the conclusions drawn for the passenger pigeon, which occurred in enormous numbers prior to its extinction in the early 20th century.
source: This echoes the conclusions drawn for the passenger pigeon (Murray et al., 2017), which occurred in enormous numbers prior to its extinction in the early 20th century.
evidence: This is a comparison with another species, supported by citation.

claim: The findings emphasise the need for thorough monitoring of commercially harvested species, particularly in poorly researched environments such as our oceans.
source: Our findings emphasise the need for thorough monitoring of commercially harvested species, particularly in poorly researched environments such as our oceans.
evidence: This is a conservation implication drawn from the study.

claim: Thorough monitoring will lay the platform for sustainable ecosystems and ensure the evidence-based conservation management of biodiversity.
source: This will lay the platform for sustainable ecosystems and ensure the evidence-based conservation management of biodiversity.
evidence: This is a statement about the benefits of monitoring.

claim: Great auk material for ancient DNA analyses was obtained from various institutions.
source: We obtained great auk material for ancient DNA (aDNA) analyses from various institutions (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This describes the sample sources.

claim: Samples were chosen to represent individuals from the major centres of the former geographic distribution of the species, spanning as wide a time period as possible.
source: Samples were chosen to represent individuals from the major centres of the former geographic distribution of the species (Figure 1), spanning as wide a time period as possible (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This describes the sampling strategy.

claim: The samples range from about 170 years old to about 13,000–15,000 years old.
source: The samples range from about 170 years old to about 13,000–15,000 years old.
evidence: This describes the temporal range of the samples.

claim: Sample dates are stratigraphically assigned (archaeological material), based on documented information (e.g., dates on which mounted specimens were killed), or estimated from known site information to give dated constraints.
source: Sample dates are stratigraphically assigned (archaeological material), based on documented information (e.g., dates on which mounted specimens were killed), or estimated from known site information to give dated constraints (e.g., Funk Island material was collected from the top layers of the islands, so the bones are most likely from individuals killed during the intense hunting period that began ~500 years ago).
evidence: This describes how sample dates were determined.

claim: Funk Island material was collected from the top layers of the islands, so the bones are most likely from individuals killed during the intense hunting period that began about 500 years ago.
source: Sample dates are stratigraphically assigned (archaeological material), based on documented information (e.g., dates on which mounted specimens were killed), or estimated from known site information to give dated constraints (e.g., Funk Island material was collected from the top layers of the islands, so the bones are most likely from individuals killed during the intense hunting period that began ~500 years ago).
evidence: This is an inference about the age of Funk Island samples based on their stratigraphic position.

claim: All laboratory work prior to polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification was carried out in the designated aDNA laboratories of the Natural History Museum of Denmark and the University of Otago.
source: All laboratory work prior to polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification was carried out in the designated aDNA laboratories of the Natural History Museum of Denmark and the University of Otago.
evidence: This describes the laboratory procedures.

claim: Strict aDNA protocols were followed to avoid contamination.
source: Strict aDNA protocols were followed to avoid contamination.
evidence: This describes the laboratory procedures.

claim: For each DNA extraction and library build, no-template controls were used to test for contamination by exogenous DNA.
source: For each DNA extraction and library build, no-template controls were used to test for contamination by exogenous DNA.
evidence: This describes the quality control procedures.

claim: All post-PCR work was carried out in separate laboratory facilities.
source: All post-PCR work was carried out in separate laboratory facilities (Knapp et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the laboratory procedures, supported by citation.

claim: Genomic DNA was extracted from 20 to 60 mg of bone powder using the method described by Dabney et al. (2013).
source: Genomic DNA was extracted from 20 to 60 mg of bone powder (Supplementary file 1b) using the method described by Dabney et al. (2013).
evidence: This describes the DNA extraction method, supported by citation.

claim: Single-stranded sequencing libraries were prepared from aDNA extracts following the protocol by Gansauge and Meyer (2013), with modifications as described by Bennett et al. (2014).
source: Single-stranded sequencing libraries were prepared from aDNA extracts following the protocol by Gansauge and Meyer (2013), with modifications as described by Bennett et al. (2014).
evidence: This describes the library preparation method, supported by citations.

claim: For some samples, double-stranded libraries were also built using the protocol described by Meyer and Kircher (2010).
source: For some samples, double-stranded libraries were also built using the protocol described by Meyer and Kircher (2010) (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This describes the library preparation method, supported by citation.

claim: Hybridisation capture was used to enrich libraries for great auk mitochondrial DNA following the MYcroarray MYbaits Sequence Enrichment protocol v2.3.1.
source: Hybridisation capture was used to enrich libraries for great auk mitochondrial DNA following the MYcroarray MYbaits Sequence Enrichment protocol v2.3.1 (MYcroarray MYbaits, 2014).
evidence: This describes the enrichment method.

claim: Samples were sequenced on Illumina platforms (HiSeq 2500 and MiSeq) at the Danish National High-Throughput DNA Sequencing Centre or by New Zealand Genomics Limited.
source: Samples were sequenced on Illumina platforms (HiSeq 2500 and MiSeq; further details in Supplementary file 1b) at the Danish National High-Throughput DNA Sequencing Centre or by New Zealand Genomics Limited.
evidence: This describes the sequencing methods and facilities.

claim: Read processing of demultiplexed sequence data was performed using the PALEOMIX v1.2.5 pipeline.
source: Read processing of demultiplexed sequence data was performed as described by Thomas et al. (2017) using the PALEOMIX v1.2.5 pipeline (Schubert et al., 2014), details of which can be found in Appendix 5.
evidence: This describes the bioinformatics methods, supported by citations.

claim: A Bayesian phylogenetic analysis of the mitogenome sequences from the 25 dated samples was performed to reconstruct the demographic history of the great auk through time.
source: To reconstruct the demographic history of the great auk through time, we performed a Bayesian phylogenetic analysis of the mitogenome sequences from the 25 dated samples ('dated' being defined here as those with associated date information, such as stratigraphically assigned dates; undated refers to those for which there is no associated dating information, such as the Funk Island samples) (Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: This describes the demographic analysis method.

claim: The sequence alignment was analysed using BEAST 1.8.4.
source: The sequence alignment was analysed using BEAST 1.8.4 (Drummond et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the analysis software, supported by citation.

claim: The exponential-growth coalescent tree prior with a positive growth rate yielded a higher marginal likelihood than the constant-size tree prior.
source: The exponential-growth coalescent tree prior with a positive growth rate yielded a higher marginal likelihood than the constant-size tree prior, suggesting that it was the best model of population dynamics in the great auk.
evidence: This is a result from the model comparison analysis.

claim: The posterior distribution of the population growth rate was highly right-skewed with a mode very close to zero.
source: However, the posterior distribution of the population growth rate was highly right-skewed with a mode very close to zero, so we conservatively used the constant-size coalescent tree prior for our analysis.
evidence: This is a result from the Bayesian analysis.

claim: The constant-size coalescent tree prior was conservatively used for the analysis.
source: However, the posterior distribution of the population growth rate was highly right-skewed with a mode very close to zero, so we conservatively used the constant-size coalescent tree prior for our analysis.
evidence: This describes the model choice for the analysis.

claim: A second analysis was performed in BEAST, in which the 16 undated mitogenomes were included in the data set.
source: A second analysis was performed in BEAST, in which the 16 undated mitogenomes were included in the data set.
evidence: This describes an additional analysis performed.

claim: A uniform prior of either (0,1000) or (0,5000) was specified for the ages of the undated mitogenomes, depending on independent information about the context of the samples.
source: A uniform prior of either (0,1000) or (0,5000) was specified for the ages of these mitogenomes, depending on independent information about the context of the samples (Shapiro et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the priors used in the analysis, supported by citation.

claim: The extended data set was still best described by a constant-size coalescent prior.
source: The extended data set was still best described by a constant-size coalescent prior.
evidence: This is a result from the analysis with the extended dataset.

claim: Population structure was investigated by inferring a haplotype network using median joining in PopART.
source: Population structure was investigated by inferring a haplotype network using median joining (Bandelt et al., 1999) in PopART (Leigh and Bryant, 2015).
evidence: This describes the network analysis method, supported by citations.

claim: Genetic diversity through space and time was visualised using statistical parsimony and a temporal haplotype network, as implemented in TempNet.
source: Genetic diversity through space and time was visualised using statistical parsimony and a temporal haplotype network, as implemented in TempNet (Prost and Anderson, 2011) (see Appendix 7 for details on TempNet age categories and Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: This describes the network analysis method, supported by citation.

claim: A population viability analysis was performed using the software Vortex 10.2.8.0 to estimate the number of great auks that were hunted annually and the rate at which a given intensity of hunting would result in population collapse and extinction.
source: We performed a population viability analysis using the software Vortex 10.2.8.0 (Lacy and Pollak, 2014) in order to estimate the number of great auks that were hunted annually, as well as the rate at which a given intensity of hunting would result in population collapse and extinction.
evidence: This describes the population viability analysis method, supported by citation.

claim: Two GPS-equipped drifting capsules were released on 10th January 2016 from a helicopter around 40 km southeast of the Reykjanes peninsula (southwestern Iceland).
source: Two GPS-equipped drifting capsules were released on 10th January 2016 from a helicopter around 40 km southeast of the Reykjanes peninsula (southwestern Iceland).
evidence: This describes the GPS capsule deployment.

claim: Each of the capsules contained a North Star TrackPack GPS tracking device, which uploaded precise location data six times a day for up to two years, through the GlobalStar satellite network.
source: Each of the capsules contained a North Star TrackPack GPS tracking device (https://www.northstarst.com/asset-trackers/trackpack/), which uploaded precise location data six times a day for up to two years, through the GlobalStar satellite network.
evidence: This describes the GPS tracking technology used.
